cases.title: Padma Bridge Rail Link: Gopibagh Harijan colony demolished
cases.place: South Kamalapur (Gopibagh TT Para) Railway Colony, Dhaka, Bangladesh
cases.point: Approximate: Kamalapur railway station, Dhaka (OpenStreetMap way 429426172). The South Kamalapur colony, known as Gopibagh TT Para, stands beside the station at the Dhaka end of the rail link.

lenders.name: Export-Import Bank of China
lenders.role: US$2,667,940,000 preferential buyer's credit signed with the Government of Bangladesh on 27 April 2018: 2% interest, six-year grace period, 20-year maturity, 0.25% management fee, 0.25% commitment fee, Bangladesh loan number B1120180427A. Disbursement reached 20% (US$533,588,000) by 30 June 2020 and 40.4% (US$1,079,727,000) by 30 June 2021, with no repayments made by that date, according to Bangladesh's Economic Relations Division (AidData record 52663).

cases.conditions: The credit financed 85% of a US$3,138,750,000 contract signed in August 2016 between the Government of Bangladesh and China Railway Engineering Corporation; Bangladesh pays the remaining 15%, US$470.81 million. China Eximbank disagreed with the government over the cost of land acquisition and cut the promised loan by 15%, from about Tk247.49 billion to Tk210.36 billion, and turned a soft loan into a preferential buyer's credit, so the government's own share rose from Tk102 billion to Tk190.43 billion. To get the credit signed, the government approved a separate China Eximbank loan of RMB 1,547,071,939.09 for a telecommunications project 'on an urgent basis', because delay on that loan was holding up this one (AidData).

companies.name: China Railway Engineering Corporation (CREC)
companies.role: General engineering, procurement and construction contractor for the 172 km Dhaka-Jessore line (AidData)
companies.desc: State-owned holding company under the supervision of China's State Council and the major shareholder of its subsidiary China Railway Group Limited; one of the world's largest transportation infrastructure contractors (Wikipedia). China Railway First Group, a subsidiary of China Railway Group Limited, is also involved in implementation (AidData).

companies.name: Bangladesh Railway
companies.role: Executing agency on behalf of the government; its staff and the project carried out the colony evictions (AidData; The Daily Star)
companies.desc: The state railway operator. Its sponsoring ministry for this project is Bangladesh's Ministry of Railways, and after the loan was signed construction was placed under a Fast Track Project Monitoring Committee headed by the prime minister (AidData). The colony the evictions cleared was railway land, and its residents worked for generations as cleaners under the railway authorities (The Daily Star).

cases.community: The line's Dhaka end runs through the South Kamalapur Railway Colony at Gopibagh, known as the TT Para sweeper colony, where Harijan and Telugu families have worked as cleaners in Dhaka for generations after their ancestors were brought from India in 1835. The Business Standard reported on 7 October 2019 that the colony's houses were demolished on 22 January 2019 for the Padma bridge rail link project and that 108 Harijan families had been living in the open since; it reported that the entire colony was not demolished and that the permanent workers' houses still stood, that one joint family of 27 people was crammed into three rooms, and that only four of the colony's ten shared bathrooms remained intact. The Daily Star reported on 28 April 2023 that 112 families were evicted in the first phase in 2019, that project staff listed the families and promised rehabilitation, and that nothing had been done to rehabilitate them; the old Shitala temple on the site was demolished at the same time. The same report says 27 more families were evicted 'last December' and that project officials verbally told them 40 more families would be evicted at any time. It reported, from Nirmal Chandra Das of the Bangladesh Harijan Oikya Parishad, that around 55 Harijan houses had been demolished and 35 partly demolished. Residents said they were told they would be rehabilitated and compensated first and were then evicted without notice, that no one outside the colony will rent to them, and that three or four families are now sharing one house.
cases.displaced_label: families evicted in the first phase in 2019 (The Daily Star)
cases.displaced_note: The Daily Star of 28 April 2023 gives 112 families evicted in the first phase in 2019 and 27 more evicted 'last December'. The Business Standard of 7 October 2019 gives 108 Harijan families living in the open after the demolition of 22 January 2019. For the later round of demolitions the counts are of houses, not families: around 55 demolished and 35 partly demolished, from Nirmal Chandra Das of the Bangladesh Harijan Oikya Parishad via The Daily Star.
cases.outcome: The project director, Md Afzal Hossain, said most of the colony's residents were living there illegally, that many were retired railway staff or worked for the city corporation or private companies, and that those living there legally would be rehabilitated in a building being prepared at Shahjahanpur Railway Colony, to which they would be shifted as soon as possible. Leaders of the Bangladesh Hindu Buddhist Christian Oikya Parishad visited the colony and called eviction without rehabilitation illegal and inhumane (The Daily Star, April 2023).

TT Para sweeper colony evicted without notice, rehabilitation

cases.confidence_note: Two newspapers report the demolitions and their figures count different things: 112 is The Daily Star's count of families evicted in the first phase, 108 is The Business Standard's count of families living in the open after the demolition of 22 January 2019. Neither the lender nor the railway has published a figure for how many were evicted or rehabilitated. The project director disputes that most of the residents had a legal right to live there, and The Business Standard reported that the permanent railway workers' houses were not demolished.
cx: Padma Bridge Rail Link Project preferential buyer's credit
cases.whole: The credit pays for a 172 km broad-gauge line from Dhaka to Jessore across the Padma Bridge, with 215.22 km of track including loops and sidings, 14 new stations, 100 coaches and the acquisition of 1,796 acres of land. Implementation began on 3 July 2018 with completion intended for June 2022; by November 2020 the works were 28.28% complete and the completion date had moved to June 2024. AidData says construction was expected to affect the living accommodation of 7,705 people, which is the project's own estimate of people affected and not a count of people moved.

cases.title: Thar Coal Block-I: land taken at Varvai, Tilvai and Bhave Jo Tar
cases.place: Varvai, Tilvai and Bhave Jo Tar, Thar Coal Block-I, Tharparkar, Sindh, Pakistan
cases.point: Thar Block I power plant site, operator Shanghai Electric Power Company Limited (OpenStreetMap way 859911854, centre of the polygon). The villages named sit inside and beside the Block-I mining area; the plant stands next to Bhave Jo Tar.

lenders.name: China Development Bank
lenders.role: Party to a US$1.43 billion syndicated buyer's credit with Thar Coal Block-I Power Generation Company (Private) Limited, insured by Sinosure. AidData's record dates the signing to 6 March 2020 in its description, while its staff comments say the precise loan commitment date is unknown and give three other dates from three sources: financial close on 31 December 2019, financial close in February 2020, and the syndicated loan agreement signed in January 2020; AidData has coded the commitment date as 31 December 2019. Its share of the syndicate is not reported and AidData assumes US$358.5 million (AidData record 53674). The People's Map of Global China, citing Global Energy Monitor, says China Development Bank, China Eximbank, ICBC and Habib Bank each provided US$358 million for the power plant and that financial close was reached in March 2020. No lead arranger is named in these sources.

lenders.name: Industrial and Commercial Bank of China
lenders.role: AidData's staff comments say ICBC 'reportedly contributed $358.5 million to the $1.43 billion syndicated loan (i.e. one-quarter of the face value of the loan)' and that the contributions of the other three lenders are unknown (AidData record 92627). The People's Map of Global China, citing Global Energy Monitor, says ICBC also agreed a US$1 billion loan for the mining operations.

lenders.name: Export-Import Bank of China
lenders.role: Party to the same US$1.43 billion syndicate; its share is not reported and AidData assumes US$358.5 million (AidData record 92628).

lenders.name: Habib Bank Limited
lenders.role: Pakistani bank in the same syndicate. AidData records its share as unknown; Global Energy Monitor, via The People's Map of Global China, gives US$358 million.

cases.conditions: The loan proceeds were to finance two engineering, procurement and construction contracts signed on 17 April 2019 between Sino Sindh Resources and two Shanghai Electric companies, worth US$434,750,358 and US$467,956,549. Pakistan guaranteed payment by the state power purchaser and guaranteed a 20% return on equity, and allowed the project company to mortgage 232.32 acres inside Block-I to its lenders. Shanghai Electric agreed to provide US$478 million of equity. AidData assumes a Pakistani sovereign guarantee on the loan, because official Chinese and Pakistani sources say all Chinese state loans to independent power projects in Pakistan carry one, and it assumes the borrowing terms match those in the national regulator's upfront tariff approval for the project: 10-year maturity, four-year grace period and 4.95% interest (AidData).

companies.name: Shanghai Electric Group Company Limited
companies.role: Owner of the power plant through Thar Coal Block-I Power Generation Company (Private) Limited, which is held 99.9997% by Shanghai Electric Investment (Dubai) Limited. AidData says Shanghai Electric agreed in September 2018 to become the controlling shareholder of the mine operator; The People's Map of Global China calls Sino Sindh Resources a subsidiary of Shanghai Electric Group 'since 2019' in its project summary and says 'in 2020 it became a subsidiary of Shanghai Electric' in its text
companies.desc: Chinese multinational power generation and electrical equipment manufacturer headquartered in Shanghai, tracing its roots to 1880 (Wikipedia). The People's Map of Global China describes it as a Shanghai Municipality-owned enterprise. Its subsidiaries Shanghai Electric Engineering Design Company Limited and Shanghai Electric Hong Kong International Engineering Company Limited hold the plant's construction contracts.

companies.name: Sino Sindh Resources (Pvt) Ltd (SSRL)
companies.role: Holder of the 30-year mining lease for Thar Coalfield Block-I awarded in October 2011 and mine operator. Its own press release says the company funded the villagers' relocation compensation; The People's Map of Global China says the government has been paying the compensation (Business Recorder; The People's Map of Global China)
companies.desc: Pakistan-registered mining company. The People's Map of Global China says it used to be a subsidiary of the privately owned Dongfang Hengxin Capital Holding Group and became a subsidiary of Shanghai Electric in 2020; AidData calls it a subsidiary of Global Mining (China) and says it was owned 55% by Global Mining China, 40% by Asiapak Investments and 5% by a Dubai-based company before Shanghai Electric took control. It is developing the open-pit lignite mine, with an output of 7.8 million tonnes a year, that feeds the power plant (AidData; The People's Map of Global China).

cases.community: Nine villages inside the Block-I project area - Varvai, Male Jo Tar, Saren Jo Tar, Sinhar Vikio, Ajbe Jo Tar, Khario Ghulam Shah, Tilvai, Bhave Jo Tar and Shahmir Vikio or Qurban Vikio - had 1,013 households and 7,566 people at the 1998 census. By September 2020 most of the land in Varvai, Tilvai and Bhave Jo Tar had been acquired. Compensation was paid at 180,000 rupees an acre, and only for land recorded in the survey: land tilled under government lease, called Yaksaala, and common grazing land, called Gowchar, are officially government land and nothing was paid for them, although local people treat them as their own property. Families in Varvai and Tilvai were to be paid a lump sum of 4.2 million rupees for each house, but many were paid only a small part of what they were owed and did not have the cash to cover the cost of resettling. At Bhave Jo Tar, next to the power plant, acquisition began in January 2018 and was almost complete by September 2021, and the families had not left because their compensation was only part paid. Residents of Khario Ghulam Shah are to stay in their village with little or no land left to till or to graze animals on, and most households there live on livestock. The company fenced village land with barbed wire and set up a checkpoint, restricting people's movement. At Kohli Para, a neighbourhood of the poorest landless Kohli families next to the plant, the company decided not to acquire land it needed for neither mine nor plant, and barbed wire, CCTV cameras and floodlights now enclose the neighbourhood on three sides, with hundreds of company workers walking through daily; women who used to graze animals and work in the fields stay in their houses (The People's Map of Global China, profile by the Rural Development Policy Institute, updated 7 December 2021). Sino Sindh Resources said in November 2021 that 266 families from Wervai and 184 from Tilwayo, 450 in all, would each receive 4.25 million rupees to move outside the mining area, that most had already built houses outside it and had started moving in, and that the company had paved roads and built a school, mosque and temple where they had moved. In August 2022 Sindh's energy minister told the chief minister that two villages had been affected by the work, that Shanghai Electric had paid 50% of the cost of the houses for the affected people and would pay the rest as work progressed, and and the company's president said land acquisition was not complete, to which the minister replied that most of the land acquisition matters had been solved and only 660 acres of Naqboli land were pending (The Express Tribune).
cases.ecosystem: The open-pit mine strips successive layers of soil across the block. The Environmental and Social Impact Assessment report on Thar Coal Mining in Sinhar Vikian Varvai Block-I puts the block at 155 square kilometres and NS Energy at 122, both as cited by The People's Map of Global China; AidData also gives approximately 122 square kilometres. Drought-resilient plants whose deep roots reach the aquifer provide the fodder that local livestock depend on. Residents of Khario Ghulam Shah, next to the mine, said dust and noise from round-the-clock excavation and trucks had become permanent, that the noise kept them awake and that respiratory illness was increasing among children and older people (The People's Map of Global China).
cases.suppression: In January and February 2021, 300 residents of Kohli Para held an 11-day protest outside the press club in Islamkot over the loss of privacy caused by the fencing, cameras and floodlights. In July 2020 people from Khario Ghulam Shah protested over the loss of their old paths and roads and over hiring. In January 2021 workers sacked from the mining company protested at the Engro roundabout in Islamkot, saying 150 had been dismissed without notice and refused severance and other dues (The People's Map of Global China).
cases.displaced_note: No count of families actually moved is agreed between the two accounts. Sino Sindh Resources said in November 2021 that 450 families from two villages had been compensated to move and that most had started moving into new houses. The People's Map of Global China recorded in a profile updated on 7 December 2021 that physical displacement had not yet taken place in Varvai, Tilvai and Bhave Jo Tar and that compensation was part paid. The 1,013 households and 7,566 people of the nine villages are a 1998 census count of people in the project area, not a count of people moved.
cases.outcome: The People's Map of Global China records that no official land acquisition and resettlement plan for Block-I has been published and that the government and local people disagree over how land is categorised. Villagers asked for the land to be leased from them with royalties on the coal, and for replacement grazing land; none of those demands was met. Several relocation sites were proposed, including Khario Ghulam Shah, Malhaytar and Mari Tar, and people said the land there was not enough; residents of Varvai judged the nearby model village poorly built and asked for cash instead. In August 2022 the chief minister of Sindh pressed Shanghai Electric to speed up building the residential colony so affected families could move in (The Express Tribune). Mining began in October 2019, about 40% of the mine work was complete by February 2021, and commercial operation of the plant was expected in February 2023 (AidData).

cases.confidence_note: The findings that compensation was only part paid and that leased and common grazing land was paid nothing come from one source: a field profile by the Rural Development Policy Institute, based on its author's 2019 fieldwork and interviews, published on The People's Map of Global China. The company's own statement says 450 families were each paid 4.25 million rupees and had started moving into new houses. The Express Tribune's account, that half the cost of the houses had been paid and that land acquisition was not complete, sits closer to the profile than to the company statement, while the energy minister in the same meeting said most land acquisition matters had been solved. The same profile says the Senhri Dars model village was built for people displaced from Block-I, while The Guardian places Sehnri Dars in Block II.
cx: Thar Block-1 integrated coal mine and power project syndicated loan
cases.whole: The project pairs an open-pit lignite mine producing 7.8 million tonnes a year with a 1,320 MW power station about 5 km from the pithead, whose output is sold to Pakistan's Central Power Purchasing Agency under a power purchase agreement signed on 27 August 2019 with a guaranteed 20% return on equity. AidData puts the total cost at US$1.9122 billion. The People's Map of Global China puts it at US$2.5 billion, split US$1.44 billion for the plant and US$1.08 billion for the mine. AidData says 4,767 people were employed on the project, 1,381 of them Chinese and 3,386 Pakistani; the People's Map profile records that local people said the skilled and senior jobs went to people from outside Thar.

fields_add.conditions: Chinese state banks joined the financing in 2016. Bank of China reportedly put US$425 million into the US$1 billion, five-year tranche of a US$2.5 billion syndicated loan to Formosa Ha Tinh (Cayman) Limited, the plant's Cayman Islands holding company; that tranche carried LIBOR plus 1.4%, and Mizuho and Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corp were in it. The other tranche, US$1.5 billion over seven years, carried LIBOR plus 1.58%, and AidData's known participants in it are Bank of Taiwan, DBS, Hua Nan Commercial Bank, Mega International Commercial Bank and Taipei Fubon Bank. China Eximbank lent RMB 400 million to Hung Nghiep Formosa Ha Tinh Steel Limited Company for the plant's two blast furnaces, built by Metallurgical Corporation of China; one of the furnaces was put into operation on 29 May 2017 and the second on 18 May 2019. AidData dates both Chinese loans to 2016 without giving a month, so whether either was signed before or after the discharge of April to June 2016 is not established (AidData).
fields_add.outcome: The plant restarted on 29 May 2017 after the halt that followed the discharge, and a dust explosion hit the complex the next day (AidData).

fields_add.conditions: China Development Bank's US$3.9675 billion loan of 14 May 2017 was split in two tranches: a US dollar tranche of US$2.3805 billion at 2% interest and a renminbi tranche worth US$1.587 billion at 3.46%, each with a 40-year maturity and a ten-year grace period, and neither carrying a sovereign guarantee (AidData records 61320 and 61321). The first disbursement, US$170 million, did not occur until May 2018.

The commercial contract behind the credit, signed on 14 February 2006 between Myanmar's Hydroelectric Power Department and Yunnan Machinery and Equipment Import and Export Corporation, was worth US$80 million. YMEC reportedly provided the department a supplier credit and financed it with an export seller's credit from China Eximbank; the face value of that credit is not reported, and AidData estimates it at 85% of the contract because that is the bank's standard share (AidData record 35828).

fields_add.community: A worker died in 2021. The Express Tribune reported on 2 July 2021 that a worker employed by a coal company who was beaten by the company's security guards had died of his injuries in a hospital in Hyderabad on the Wednesday night, and that the family of the dead man, Dodo Bheel, staged a sit-in on the Mithi-Islamkot road in Thar Coal Block II at Islamkot; it reported that he was among almost a dozen people suspected of stealing iron from the company and that his family said he was held in illegal detention for some days and tortured. The Human Rights Commission of Pakistan said Dodo Bheel was tortured by Sindh Engro Coal Mining Company's security guards. Dawn, as reported by ANI, said he was one of several workers detained by company security guards for 14 days for interrogation over the theft of scrap from a store in the Thar Coal project's Block-II, according to his family, and that the guards handed him to the Islamkot police when his condition turned critical. ARY News reported that he died on the night between 30 June and 1 July. The company said a third-party contract worker had died at Block II, that the accused personnel had been suspended, that an internal fact-finding was under way and that it was cooperating with the police (SECMC response of 20 July 2021, via the Business and Human Rights Resource Centre).
fields_add.suppression: Police baton-charged and teargassed the Bheel community's sit-in over the death. The Human Rights Commission of Pakistan said it was outraged, backed the demand for an immediate and impartial inquiry, and called the arrest of protesters under the Anti-Terrorist Act 'a case of custodial overreach'. Dawn, as reported by ANI, said police moved in late on the Sunday, began baton-charging the protesters and tried to arrest some of the 150 protesters booked under sections of the Anti-Terrorism Act and the Pakistan Penal Code, and that eight security guards were detained for interrogation but those named in the police report were not among them. Aaj English TV reported on 5 July 2021 that videos of Islamkot police hitting people with batons had circulated, and that the Tharparkar senior superintendent of police was reported to have threatened the protesters with strict action if they did not end the protest.
fields_add.outcome: The Business and Human Rights Resource Centre asked ICBC, China Development Bank, China Construction Bank, China Machinery Engineering Corporation, State Power Investment Corporation and State Power International Mengdong to respond to the reports about the death and the policing of the protests; it recorded no response from any of them, and only Sindh Engro Coal Mining Company replied. Its item of 16 July 2021 is headed on the mining company refusing to cooperate with the fact-finding mission, and says the company was invited to respond to allegations that it had tortured and killed a worker and that it was advised not to cooperate in a fact-finding probe; its timeline also carries a report of 10 July 2021 that the Sindh government asked company officials not to meet the members of the fact-finding probe.

extend.killed_note_replace: One worker's death. The Express Tribune reported on 2 July 2021 that a worker beaten by a coal company's security guards died of his injuries in a hospital in Hyderabad, and placed the family's sit-in in Thar Coal Block II at Islamkot; the dead man was Dodo Bheel, a third-party contract worker at the mine. His family and the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan say he was tortured by Sindh Engro Coal Mining Company security guards after being held for 14 days over the theft of scrap from a store at Block-II; ARY News gives the death as the night between 30 June and 1 July. Islamkot police booked five guards, eight guards were detained for interrogation without those named in the police report among them, and ARY News reported on 28 August 2021 that a court in Mithi had refused bail to the main accused. The Sindh government announced 10 million rupees for his family and the chief minister set up a committee of three ministers to investigate. No court has ruled on the cause.
